title: The alphabet and its pronunciations

objectives.can: Read Latin letters aloud in the classical or the ecclesiastical pronunciation, and say where the two differ.

explanation.summary: Latin is written in the letters you already know, but two living traditions read them aloud differently: the classical pronunciation, which aims at the sounds of Rome in the first century BC, and the ecclesiastical pronunciation, the Italian-flavoured reading used in the Church's worship. This lesson sets them side by side so that you can read the Vulgate in either.

sections.heading: Same letters, two ways of saying them
body: Most Latin letters sound much as they do in English or, better, in Italian: a, e, i, o, u are pure vowels (about 'father', 'bed', 'machine', 'for', 'food'), and every letter in a word is sounded. The difference between the two traditions lies in a small number of letters and letter-groups, set out in the first table. Its two sound columns are headed 'Sound (Classical)' and 'Sound (Ecclesiastical)'.

Neither tradition changes the word. *Lucem* is the same word, with the same meaning, whether you say 'LOO-kem' (classical) or 'LOO-chem' (ecclesiastical). You can choose the pronunciation that suits you, and the lessons of this course do not depend on the choice.

sections.heading: Soft c and g, and the letters that follow them
body: The ecclesiastical pronunciation softens c and g before the 'front' vowels e and i, and before the diphthongs ae and oe, which it says as e. So the c of *lucem* is hard in the classical reading and a 'ch' in the ecclesiastical, while the c of *lux* is hard in both. Before a, o, u or a consonant both traditions say c as k and g as the g of 'get'.
The same front-vowel rule governs sc: before e and i it becomes the 'sh' of 'shed' in the ecclesiastical pronunciation, and stays 'sk' in the classical.

sections.heading: Vowels, diphthongs and a few special groups
body: The vowels a, e, i, o, u have one sound each. The classical pronunciation also distinguishes long from short vowels, and that difference matters for accent and for verse. The editions in this library print no macrons (the bars over long vowels), so this course does not mark length; where a word's quantity matters, the lesson says so.

The diphthong au is 'ow' as in 'cow' in both traditions. In the classical reading ae is 'ai' and oe is 'oi'; in the ecclesiastical both are simply e. The edition prints the diphthong ae as the ligature æ (*cælum*, *tenebræ*) in many places.

In the classical reading ti before a vowel is just t followed by i, as in *gratia*. The ecclesiastical reading usually says it 'tsi'. The usual exceptions are where the t follows s, t or x. The ecclesiastical pronunciation also treats gn as 'ny' (so *agnus* sounds 'AH-nyoos') and leaves h silent.

sections.heading: i and j, u and v
body: The Roman alphabet did not distinguish i from j or u from v. Editors do, and not all alike. The Vulgate edition in this library prints *Jesum* and *justorum*, where other editions print *Iesum* and *iustorum*. These are one word in two spellings, not two words. Consonantal i or j is said like English y in 'yes' in both traditions. For v the traditions differ, as the table shows.

misunderstandings: The ecclesiastical pronunciation is not 'wrong Latin', and the classical one is not 'the real Latin' in the sense of a different language. They are two conventions for reading the same text aloud, and the ecclesiastical one is the tradition of the Church's use for centuries.
Changing the pronunciation does not change which word you are looking at. A word's identity lies in its letters, ending and meaning, not in how a school says it.
'Silent h' is not an instruction to drop the letter in the spelling. The h stays in *habitavit*; only the sound differs between traditions.

deeper.heading: Where the ecclesiastical pronunciation comes from
body: The ecclesiastical pronunciation is the Latin of Italy as it was spoken and sung over many centuries, and it is closely related to Italian pronunciation. Local custom differed by country for most of the Middle Ages; the Italianate form became general in Catholic worship in the twentieth century. Some scholars of the older English school, for instance, taught still other readings. This lesson describes the commonest teaching forms only; individual choirs and schools differ in small points.

paradigms.note: Both traditions say c before a, o, u or a consonant as k, and g there as in 'get'; both say au as 'ow' as in 'cow'. The classical pronunciation also keeps long and short vowels apart, which the editions do not mark.

examples.analysis: *lucem* is the accusative of *lux*, 'light'. The c stands before e, so the two traditions differ: 'LOO-kem' in the classical reading, 'LOO-chem' in the ecclesiastical. It is one word either way.

reading.why: Five short verses, full of plain words (*lux*, *vita*, *tenebræ*, *Deum*) with c before e and before other letters, and the diphthong ae. Read them aloud once in each pronunciation.
